utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I understand there's a matter that you wish to raise. We'll hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this is a matter that I should respond to in private session, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes. Private session. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit and you may continue with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Knustad.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, we left yesterday and you had told the Court that you arrived in Sarajevo in June 1995, and you said that you were positioned with the Sector Sarajevo, UNMO Sector Sarajevo. And you said that you had -- before you were transferred to Sarajevo, you underwent some training in Zagreb? And I just wanted to ask you, what kind of training did you undertake?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it was ordinary administrative checking; but besides that and based on the knowledge that UNMO headquarters in Zagreb had about the situation, we were also given some lectures in especially crater analysis after impacts. So we had some lectures on that as well in Zagreb before we went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How long did that training last for?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, let's move to Sarajevo, and please tell the Court how many UNMOs teams were there in Sarajevo at the time you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sector Sarajevo, there were four UNMO teams, each of them consisting of ten military observers from various countries. In addition to that, it was UNMO Sector headquarters in the PTT building in Sarajevo. So, in all, it was around 630 military observers, four teams; one team in the eastern part, Stari Grad area of Sarajevo; two teams in the middle part; and one team in the western part, west of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Which team were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to the team at eastern part of Sarajevo, at that time named Kilowatt Charlie 1, which had a team base in Sedrenik, and our area of responsibility was Stari Grad, the eastern part towards the Presidency and to what is now the American embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say Stari Grad, do you know the old town?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the old part of the city, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, how many UNMO members were in your team?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my team, we were most of the time ten UNMOs; but at all times, there were at least one UNMO on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who was your team leader, if you had one?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: My team leader, when I arrived, was Dutch Lieutenant-Colonel Harry Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Within your team base, did you have any observation points in and around -- well, within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team had the responsibility to man observation post at the southern part of the city, south of the district area, more specific, the Colina Kapa. And our team manned that observation post 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: For the benefit of the court, we will -- I will ask you to mark these positions on a map. But you said observation post, was there a shorthand term used to describe observation post while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was the term "observation post" shortened in a way?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't shortened. I mean, we had the responsible to man that 24 hours a day, and we shifted duties every 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I think what he meant was whether there was another term that was used to describe "observation post" as maybe an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. It was named in military terms, OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your guidance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The team based in Sedrenik, what was that called?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was called Kilowatt Charlie 1, KC1, in the Sedrenik area?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the observation post in Colina Kapa, what that was called?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was called OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: At the time that you arrived Sarajevo, were there any United Nations military observers in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were no military observers in Republika Srpska, and the reason for that was that UN withdraw all military observers under Serb-held territory after the hostage crisis in May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: As an UNMO in your team, describe briefly the tasks that you would undertake?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main purpose of much UN Military Observer is obviously to supervise a cease-fire. At this point, there was no real cease-fire, at least not in Sector Sarajevo. Our main task, as military observers, is to observe, investigate, and report. And as the situation was in Sarajevo, a lot of our duties went to observation and investigation of shelling and sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your approach, generally, in the UNMO's approach to their work, were you guided by any the principles or standards in your work?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most important principle was that we had to be 100 per cent impartial, and for a profession officer that is not a very difficult task. Even at the stage, we were only on the -- on the Bosnian government side as military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did the thoroughness or the rigour of your investigations depend upon the ethnicity of the victims in any way?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the situation in Sarajevo was in 1995 and even before that, it's a mixed of ethnicities. There are both Bosnian Muslims, there are Serb Orthodox, and there are Croat Catholics, all mixed. And there were, at the time I was in Sarajevo from June 1995 until December 1995, also mixed marriages. And as I can recall, the people of Sarajevo mainly considered themselves Sarajevo people and were not at that point very concerned about which ethnicity they belonged to, to use that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it that in your investigations, it did not matter whether the victims were Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Croat, or Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us, in our investigation, it certainly didn't matter. But an important part of our task was to confirm casualties, and we quickly learned how we could identify the different ethnicities by the name. So it was not difficult to see whether it was Serb, Croat, or Bosnian Muslim; that was a casualty in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In your investigations, did you also determine, at least with respect to shelling, the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direction of fire was probably one of the most important aspects of our investigation, and the way we did that was based on our training in crater analysis and the crater that is caused by an impact from either artillery or mortar. And based on that, we could tell with quite a good certainty which direction it was fired from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned mortars. Do you know what a modified air bomb is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know what a modified air bomb is, and we were briefed about that from Sector Sarajevo. That is mainly a bomb meant to be dropped from aircraft; but in this case, the Bosnian Serb modified those bombs with a propulsion device so that it could be fired from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Given your experience with artillery pieces that you told the Court in the beginning, what can you say about the accuracy or inaccuracy of these modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: These modified air bombs are highly inaccurate, and that's because there is no really steering device on them. You can only direct them in a certain direction. I can't see any certain military purpose of these kind of weapons. They also were very slow in flight and had a considerable and very noticeable sound during the flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to give a figure as to the -- well, let's say the impact, the radius of impact of a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to say, because they are -- well, let me use the term, homemade devices. But I wouldn't think that it would be possible to -- to have the impact in anything less than one kilometre accuracy as a diameter of the impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was there a term or a phrase that the UNMOs gave to these modified air bombs while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any special term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was their limit? How far could they travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it depends on the propulsion device on them, but the knowledge we had at the moment was that they couldn't be fired from -- from more than maximum six, 7.000 metres and, as I said, highly inaccurate. I would say it's mainly a weapon to create fear and not for any particular military purpose, based on my knowledge as an officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you also said that they were very slow-moving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On one occasion, I witnessed myself a modified air bomb fired from an area we called Sharpstone, which was just a few hundred metres from our team base; and we could see it during the first part of the flight, but we didn't see where it impacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But are you able to say anything about the speed at which it travelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is very difficult to determine, but it was certainly a lot slower than, for example, a 120-millimetre mortar grenade. But I can't be more accurate about the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, just to continue with the President's question. Many expert witnesses told us about these modified air bombs, and you also are saying that they were quite slow. What was the propulsion system like? Was it a rocket? A drone? How did they -- how high did they go into flight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The propulsion system was a rocket that was detached to the bomb itself, and I don't have any details, but are placed on a launching device so that it could be just fired out in the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, based on your previous answers and also your experience, what can say about the appropriateness of -- of the use of modified air bombs in an urban environment like Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to put it mildly, it's highly inappropriate because, as I stated, this is not a weapon that has any the direct military purposes. And any forces deployed around Sarajevo would have to know that they there would be a lot of collateral damage, as we call it, a lot of civilian inflicted by the use of these kind of modified air bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say it was not a weapon that had a direct military purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Normally, in military terms, you would have a specific target. If you fire artillery or a mortar, you do it towards a target which has a position. With the inaccuracy of the modified air bombs, there couldn't possibly be more than an area target. And in a populated city, full of civilian houses very close to each other, it's obvious that the use of such a weapon would also cause a lot of destruction and damage on the civilian population and infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may be more accurate to say it had no proper military purpose, but that's just a nicety. I understand what you what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, with respect to modified air bombs and mortars, can you tell the Trial Chamber roughly how many incidents did you investigate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a fairly high number of incidents. I arrived in Sector Sarajevo on the 21st of June; and on a normal day, there would be more than 100 impacts around the city, both from artillery and from mortar and from rockets. Due to this, it's obvious that four teams of UNMOs wouldn't be able to conduct investigation of all those impacts, so we had to prioritise; and in that sense, we had to make hard priorities and the priorities were impacts that inflicted casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So just sticking to the incidents that you yourself investigated with your team, what can you say about the character of targets that you investigated?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the first glance, the targets might seem random; but after being there a while and getting some experience on the -- on the investigations, it was obvious that some of those areas that were targeted were areas where people would gather. That would be like areas to pick up food, areas where you could collect water, areas where there was narrows in the roads that people had to do go through. It was also a lot of investigations in -- in parks, in cemeteries, and also around the Kosovo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to a specific incident. Firstly, do you recall an incident on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall this -- this special incident on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And where did that incident occur?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one impact in the Markale area in the middle of Sarajevo city, and in our team's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, I assumed duty on the mentioned OP1, around 9.00 in the morning; and during the morning, which was a very clear and bright morning, without very much wind, I was on duty together with an UNMO colleague from OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who was your UNMO colleague?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Major Paul Conway from Ireland.?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was there anybody else with you and Mr. Conway?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also an interpreter since we always brought an interpreter with us, both on the OP for 24 hours and when we went on parole in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you had assumed your duty at the OP1, for how long was that duty to be for?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there for 48 hours, so we relieved two UNMOs that had been there for 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you earlier told the Court that the OP1 was in Colina Kapa; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What kind of view did you have over the city and in particular the old town from that area?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military point of view, this is sort of a perfect place to have an observation post. Because covering the old part of the city, you had a very good view towards the front line on the northern end of the city and, of course, all the streets, houses, and everything happening down in the city from the old part, from Bascarsija in particular and towards Skenderija and the western part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You got there at 9.00 on the morning of the 28th; and during that time, during the morning, was there anything significant that you heard or viewed while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 28th, there had been actually for a couple of days less intensity of shelling. I noticed it was a fairly quiet day, but still we could hear a lot of noises, like the activity in the -- in the city. And -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So while you were on the observation point, did you see anything happen in the city?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, around 11.00, as I recall it, I first saw a smokestack coming up from the -- what I immediately identified to be the area of the market-place, Markale, and that is approximately 2.000 metres from the observation post. And with a sound of speed, five, six, seconds after, I heard an impact from that area that I understood came from -- from the smokestack that I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just so we're clear about the term that you used, what is a smokestack, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smokestack is the smoke that would develop from an impact of, for example, a mortar grenade or an artillery grenade, mainly grey towards black of colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would apologise. I would just ask my learned friends if they're conferring, to at least keep it quiet because it is sometimes off putting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, did you hear that, Ms. Isailovic and Mr. Tapuskovic? Your whispering is being seen as a campaign against the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That is not quite what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was being light-hearted there, but the Prosecutor was complaining about the consistent and persistent talk there. There is no need to explain anything. Just be quiet, Mr. Tapuskovic. We know that you didn't mean any disrespect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't speak English, unfortunately, and this makes my job quite difficult. I can't read the transcript, and I wanted to consult with my colleague to check whether the witness first heard the sound and then saw the smoke or vice versa. And I was merely trying to confirm that with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, please do so in a manner that is not audible. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you that. With respect to what you saw and what you heard, what was the sequence?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the OP1 position is approximately 2.000 metres from the market-place area. I observed, first, the smokestack; and since the speed the sound of speed is around 300 metres per second, it took approximately five, six seconds until I heard the impact after I saw the smokestack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did your colleague, Mr. Conway, also experience what you experienced?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Paul Conway was manning the OP itself. I observed this in the front of the house that we used as a base for our OP, which has very good view above the city as well. I knew that I had more experience as a military observer than Paul Conway; so immediately after I observed the smokestack and heard the impact, I went approximately 150 metres to the OP position, where Paul Conway was, to confirm whether he had heard and seen the same. And he confirmed to me that he had seen the same as me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Once it was established that you had both seen the same, did-- was this reported?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, it was written in the log that we kept on the observation post, and then it was reported by radio directly to the UNMO headquarters in the PTT building, as was the procedure for these kind of impacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who actually reported it to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paul Conway reported it to the headquarters via radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to show the witness 65 ter 2632, and I'm interested in showing page 11 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, do you see a document on your screen there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, on the left-hand side, do you see a reference to your observation point?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. On the first line with the day-time group, the 28/11.10, Bravo reported from OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see where it says, "105th BBD BiH?"

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is additional information that is put in from the UNMO headquarters to describe in a readable way actually where the impact was. And this refers to the headquarters of the army of BiH and 105th Brigade, which we used as a reference point in our reports to the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In this -- this reference point, does this mean that the -- the target was in fact the 105th Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not mean that was the target. We can't imagine what could have been actually the target for this impact. It's simply a name that refers to a known place, and it's a description instead of just a map reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you earlier said that your team leader was Mr. Konings; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was he involved in any way in an investigation of this incident?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I listen into, of course, the communication on the radio that also my team leader Harry Konings had, I was informed that he was task to go to the place of the impact and do the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would also like to bring up 65 ter 891, pages 37 to 42. Actually, the first three pages of this document have also been admitted as P0085, if that helps. May we go to the third page of this, please. All right. That is the chart I want to have shown. Is it possible to move it, so it can be seen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, do you see a chart on your screen there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. With the heading "crater analysis."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: At the first line of that chart, what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refers to the time of the investigation that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "the investigation that was done," are you referring to the investigation at the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the investigation on the Markale market, which -- and this is the same analysis of the impact that I stated that I observed from OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The fourth column from the left, do you see where it says "bearing."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see it's figures there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows 170 degrees plus/minus 5 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just did not understand whether the witness himself worked on this document. Is this document a result of his own research? Could the Prosecutor perhaps clarify this with the witness so that I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, did you produce this document?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't produce that document itself, but this document is from the UNMO team that I was a part of. And we conducted our duties as a team, but, obviously, this was made by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, who was actually the UNMO at the impact site.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You were just -- you were just about to -- I asked what the 170 degree, plus/minus 5 degrees indicated meant. You were about to answer, so could you please proceed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, as it is written above the bearing, meaning from which direction, they determined where the impact came from. So that means that from the impact, the direction of fire, it came from 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I was to ask you to -- to indicate this on a map using a ruler and a protractor, would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have copies of maps that I want to show the witness, and I have copies for Your Honours and counsel. I think counsel already has a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, is this a 92 ter witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, he is a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He is a live witness. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But I expect to be finished with him in the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, first of all, on that map, can you please mark the location of OP1.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you just put beside that the letters "OP" and the figure "1."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: To the -- well, can you mark the front lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor. Is there a chance that you can reduce the light on the ELMO a bit, because it's almost unreadable on -- on our screens. Yes, that's better. That's better. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Firstly, from OP1, how far were the confrontation lines from your position?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that the front part of the army of BiH confrontation line was approximately 200 metres to the south of OP1; and then, obviously, you would have some no man's land, and I would estimate and we were briefed that the Bosnian Serb front line was approximately 1500 metres south of OP1, directly to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you mark on the map the position of the Bosnian government confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's correct that everything beyond that line, as we're looking in this picture to the bottom, was territory -- was territory of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was VRS territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness has said that the positions of the army of Republika Srpska were 1800 [as interpreted] metres away from this line, did I understand that correctly? Could he draw a line to show the direction. He said that the army of Republika Srpska positions were 15 or 1800 metres away from these positions here. Could he just draw a line to show us graphically what he meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, please remember that you will have your turn to cross-examine. But if this is something which will be useful to the Chamber, I see no harm in the witness doing it. Let him do it. Yes, let the witness draw that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. I would just know, though, for the record that the witness spoke of 1500 metres, not 1800. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, and also from the 1500 metres south of OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, just to be clear, can you mark beside those lines "ABiH" and "VRS."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, with -- if it's possible with a finer pen, can you use a protractor a ruler -- well, first of all, let me ask you to identify Markale market.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked it with a cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Can you now with the protractor and ruler draw the direction 170 degrees, plus/minus 5.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, before my next set of questions, I just want to the ask you, in your experience, how many times have you heard a mortar being fired?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, my branch in -- in the navy was artillery, coast artillery. I was trained with the artillery, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether this will be benefit you as well, but why doesn't he draw a line from their observation post to Markale. I don't understand the purpose of this line. Why isn't a line drawn from the location where they had their observation post to Markale market, so that this map really serves a purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you can ask the witness to do that in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knustad, you were saying, in the navy coast artillery I was trained with..." If you could please continue?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have a lot of experience in observing impacts from my service as an artillery officer in the coast artillery. Part of the coast artillery was also mortars. It's very difficult to determine the exact number, but I have seen, observed, and heard probably a lot more than 100 mortar rounds, specifically 81-millimetre during my duty before 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What about 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have 120-millimetre mortars in our navy, but, unfortunately, I got to see a lot of 120-millimetre impacts during my service in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is the sound of a 120-millimetre mortar being fired louder or softer to a sound of a 82-millimetre [sic] mortar being fired?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: 120-millimetre is louder as well softer than an 81-millimetre. 81-millimetre will have a sharper noise than a 120-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, when you say louder, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is more decible when a 120-millimetre mortar is fired than when an 81-millimetre is being fired. I would, based on my experience, say that it's easier to hear a 120-millimetre mortar being fired on long distance than an 81-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What is the maximum distance one can be at from the place of firing the mortar where you could hear that firing sound?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been on all kind of distances referred to -- mortar fire. Everything from two metre behind to at least five, six kilometres away from the mortar. And depending on the weather conditions, the wind, and other variables, I would say it would at least be possible to hear a 120-millimetre mortar being fired, at least, let's say from a four to five kilometres distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: On the day that you saw the plume of smoke, from your position, did you hear a mortar being fired from within the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear any mortar being fired until I saw the smokestack or heard the impact on the market-place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If the mortar had been fired from within the confrontation lines along the direction of fire as you have indicated here, would you from your position have heard that mortar being fired?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly have heard any 120-millimetre mortar being fired from within the confrontation line and, in particular, in the -- direction of fire that I have indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Behind your position at OP1 in VRS territory, is the land -- is there a hill, is it elevated, or is it flat?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OP1 is located on a slope going down towards the city, with a hill behind to the south on the map. There is a ridge on the top, and behind that it's going down, again, towards the Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If the mortar had been fired from the just behind the VRS lines, would you have heard that being fired?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it's very possible that a mortar could have been fired from behind the VRS line, but I wouldn't hear it due to the configuration of the terrain and the way the sound would move behind the hill, behind my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So can we put it this way: Are you able to exclude the possibility of the mortar being fired from within the confrontation lines along that flight path?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can exclude the possibility that any mortar was fired from within the -- the ABiH territory. And I want to add to this that we, as military observers, were aware of the fact that there were speculations that the Bosnian government forces were actually firing at their own people from within the confrontation line, so these conspiracy theories and allegations we were very aware of and very observant for those kind of things when being on a duty within the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I will get to that in a moment. I asked you whether you could exclude the possibility of it being fired from within the confrontation line. Can you exclude the possibility that it was fired from outside the confrontation line; that is, in VRS territory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exclude the fact that it was fired from VRS territory and mainly because of the configuration of the terrain as I explained. Because in that case, it would have been fired from behind the hill where I was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I missed, but did he explain why he can exclude the possibility that the mortar was fired from within the ABiH territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I submit that he did, on account of -- on account of the fact that he would have been in a position to hear it, if it had been fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is, as you can see on the map, only one kilometre of distance from my position in OP1 towards the west and it's angle that I draw and where that crosses the front line of the ABiH army. So within that short distance, I can state that I would have heard any mortar fired from within that area of my position towards the angle indicating the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, you gave an answer just a moment ago about accusations or conspiracies theories the Bosnians were shelling themselves. Did you in your time in Sarajevo ever come to a conclusion or perform an investigation where this indeed took place?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did a large number of investigations, and I personally myself did a large part of those investigations within the confrontation line, and we were never able to determine that any of those investigations that we did were actually as -- an impact as a result of fire from -- from inside the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The fact that you did not hear the mortar being fired from within the confrontation lines, was that reported or relayed to the persons doing the investigation of the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I reported that to my team leader, Harry Konings, on the day after the incident, on the 29th of August. And I reported that to him, because I knew that would be very vital information in all the information covering this particular incident. And I told my team leader, Colonel Konings, that I did not hear any outgoing mortar rounds from within the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The answer which you gave previously to the Prosecutor, was that confined to investigations that you were personally involved in with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That refers to both investigations that I personally did and investigations that my team but other observers in the team did. So during my time in the team in Sarajevo, we were never able to -- to determine that any mortar or artillery was actually fired from within the confrontation line on those investigations we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, just upon your answer where you said you reported the fact that you did not hear the mortar being fired from within the confrontation lines to Mr. Konings, can I just -- if we go back to the e-court and the exhibit that is currently on the screen. If we can go two pages forward from that, please. Do you see a page there on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see a page with a point for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you go down to the paragraph which has the 2 beside it. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you see where it's the letter A?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you just read that paragraph, if you can, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the time frame of the five impacts UNMOs in the [indiscernible] team working on OP1," I can't read the next two words, "heard no outgoing mortar rounds neither from Bosnian army territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think it says, "general area."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: "General area Bistrik and Colina Kapa nor from Bosnian Serb army territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Does that reflect report that you gave to Colonel Konings?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Neither myself or Paul Conway heard any outgoing mortar rounds, and that is correct what is stated here. That is what we reported, we did not hear any outgoing round.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just inquire as to how long I've taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's good to see that you are being sensitive to the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President that is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic, you would, of course, have the same time as the Prosecutor, which is one hour. But if you need additional time, you can apply for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will decide about that later. I believe that I will need a bit more, given the examination-in-chief. But bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have our break soon, and I will be able to prepare myself over the break. I have several questions, but, first of all, thank you, Your Honours. I really am not versed in technology. Mr. Witness, could you please explain certain matters that were the subject of the examination-in-chief. Rest assured, I will not be mentioning any conspiracy theories; however, I will ask you to honour the basic principles of mathematics and other sciences which are relevant to the events in Sarajevo. I never contemplated conspiracy theories, but I will ask you to be guided in your answers by the basic scientific principles. You said that you completed training in Zagreb over the course of six days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that and that's correct, but that is in addition to the three weeks military observer course that I attended in Finland during the spring/winter of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on the eve of your departure, your speciality were craters. Is that right? And I'm speaking of the month of June 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNMO headquarters in Zagreb were very aware of the number of impacts that were in Sarajevo and other parts of the city, and that's why they consider it important that we got a refreshments of our knowledge in the conduct of crater analysis, which is the process where you determine from which direction the weapon was fired and what kind of weapon that was used based on the fragments that you would find resting on the impact site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that you took up your duties in Sarajevo, firmly believing that you would be doing your job in the most impartial of manners; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Impartiality is the basis. Impartiality the basis of the conduct of a military observer; and as I also stated, the main purpose was to supervise a cease-fire. But in this way, there was no cease-fire to supervise. But as professional officers, we would have to stick to the rule about impartiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As I understand it, you arrived in the middle of the offensive launched by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Republika Srpska army. For several day, perhaps ten days even, you did not leave the premises or could not leave your premises to attend to your duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In fact, we had a troubled trip by car from Split to Sarajevo, and we were held up in one area which is Konjic, just south-west to Sarajevo. And due to our own safety, we had to take cover over there because there was lot of fighting going on between Bosnian army forces and Serb forces in the area between ourselves and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, that was not my question. I asked you something else, and I would like you to answer that. As you arrived in Sarajevo, you were unable to carry out your duties for several days due to the fierce offensive raging at the time between the two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I arrived in Sarajevo on the 21st of July, and we arrived from Igman and had support from French battalion as protection to travel down Igman and into -- to Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In view of the fact that you arrived at the time when there was ongoing fighting and your purpose being to impartially analyse craters, did you throughout your stay in Sarajevo examine any craters caused by the Bosnia-Herzegovina side to prove your impartiality, or did you only go out into the area held by the Republika Srpska army to examine the craters there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have to prove any impartiality. But as I stated before, we had to make strong priorities as a way which impacts we would investigate. All those impacts were within the confrontation line on ABiH-held territory because, as I mentioned earlier, we as military observers were not allowed to go to the Bosnian Serb-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the early days of your stay in Sarajevo, I don't have time now to show you a document because it's in the language you don't understand. It was authored by Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time that you arrived, did you hear up to 100.000 bullets fired by the side of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm not exaggerating. I will in due time show this document to the Trial Chamber. I just wanted to know whether you had heard that at the time of the offensive of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would so happen that from the side of Sarajevo, you would hear as many as 100.000 rounds upon the areas held by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no comments as to the number of rounds. It's, obviously, impossible to count 100.000 rounds fired, but what I do confirm is that there was fighting going on along the front line around Sarajevo. That I can confirm, but not the number of sounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: . Yes, but did you hear any rounds at all, never mind how many, fired by the Bosnian Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were rounds of small arms fired from both sides. We went to sleep on small arms fire, and we woke up -- on small arms fire. It was continuous small arms fire in -- in the whole area surrounding our team base in Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know what your decision will be, what your ruling will be, but let us use this several minutes that we have before the break. The map that I showed you in private session, yesterday, will be used by the Defence with every witness, save for the victim witnesses. I ask for your leave to use it. I delivered a copy to the OTP already. By your leave, can I put several questions to this witness in relation to the map? I'm sure it is admissable. I delivered the map today. I didn't do so yesterday because I didn't have copies available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just fetch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: First, Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President I apologise, but I would -- while this is being set up, I inadvertently forgot to tender the map that the witness marked in my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I might tender that as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with the assistance of the interpreters, I will be going through this and speaking slowly. At the top, it says, "The decision by the SRK commander," do you see that? Can the interpreters -- did you hear interpretation of what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Can you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the top of the map, it says, "The decision by the SRK commander."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you can't confirm that, of course. On the left-hand side, it says -- or, rather, on the right-hand side it says, "Military secret, strictly confidential." Do you see that on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see there are Cyrillic letters there, But I'm not an expert in Cyrillics. I can't read what is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the interpreters have interpreted the text for you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom, it says, "Commander, Major-General Dragomir Milosevic." Do you agree with this, now that the interpreters have told you that this is what it says?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We cannot see what Mr. Tapuskovic is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: , And now hear it says, in the left-hand side corner that, "The commander, Lieutenant general, or rather, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic is confirming this decision."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand enough Cyrillic letters to see that that is what is written in the upper left-hand corner, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It says,"I approve this decision..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: As you arrived in Sarajevo, and I will show this to you after the break, you said that you dealt with the confrontation lines between the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that you were to mark them off. Is this what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what it means "mark them off."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's time for the break any way. I will try to specify my question after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't understand it either, so find another way to reflect what in English has been interpreted as "mark them off." We'll take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We were waiting on the technician from the audiovisual booth but I decided not to wait any longer, since the 20-minute break it expired. I just wanted to very briefly give two decisions. One relates to two motions filed on the 23rd and 24th of January by the Prosecution for admission into evidence of three written statements: W 19, W 28, and W 136. The Defence doesn't challenge the admissibility of the statements under Rule 92 ter, but it objects to the statements stating that it does not have time to cross-examine the witness. The Trial Chamber will allocate reasonable time for cross-examination based on, among other factors, the length of the examination-in-chief, the length of the 92 ter statement, and it's significance of the witness' testimony. The Trial Chamber, therefore, grants the Prosecution's motion and admits the statements of Witness 19, 28, and 36 into evidence upon fulfilment of the request. Next I wanted to refer to the Prosecution motion filed on the 5th of February, 2007, pursuant to 92 ter. And this concerns the witness John Jordan who is due to testify on Monday, the 19th of February. The Defence response is due on the 19th of February, 2007 and the Trial Chamber would like to find out from the Defence whether it will be in a position to respond by Thursday, the 15th of February to this motion. Let us know what your position is. In that event, we will then issue our decision on Friday, the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's a witness who will be taken by my colleague, so she will respond on behalf of the Defence and explain the problems involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I am not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologizes, but the microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please, start again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. So we're taking into account the decision that you just made. Now, regarding John Jordan's testimony, according to Article -- Rule 92 ter, the Defence has no objection towards that at all. Everything is fine for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us then proceed with the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have managed to regroup during the break and to organise myself, selecting only the most essential matters for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask the witness this: I have taken all material that I received from the OTP concerning this witness, including two maps, in fact, two aerial maps. I believe that the Prosecution has them in various formats, but this format can hardly be placed in e-court; and before I ask the witness anything concerning these maps, I would like them distributed to the Trial Chamber so that you can follow. These maps are part of the material that I received for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have the copies, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, you know very well what these maps depict. Did you take these photographs from an air plane, from a helicopter? Can you explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not me who has provided those images, so I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, but in addition to these photographs, did you see other photographs that cover a larger area, not only the centre of Sarajevo. On this image, we do not see anything outside this narrow area of Sarajevo. Do you know if you have made other images that include a broader area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no other images. But the maps that we used as military observers were in the scale 1:50.000, and it covered as well areas outside of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was: "Do you know if you have made other images, that include a broader area of Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally haven't made any images, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would have to ask the Prosecutor to clarify this. Do they have any maps that show a broader area? If they do, I believe it was their obligation to disclose to me all of them, not only the centre of Sarajevo. I'm taking the liberty to ask you, Your Honours, to clarify this with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have any maps which show a broader area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, indeed, we did and I handed over to counsel -- I recall about two or three days ago. In other words, this is a large-scale map -- it's a large inset of a full map of Sarajevo, which I I gave to counsel in a A3 format. I had intended to use this with the witness; but in the interests of efficiency, I did not. But counsel -- I gave him three or four more copies of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on. Mr. Tapuskovic, they have been handed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I'm asking. I want them to show you that map as well, because this one shows a very narrow area. Can they also show the small map of Sarajevo that they had given me? I am certain that they have a copy in a large format of that small map. Could they show the small map to the witness, so that I can ask him questions of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what is it exactly that you want? Because I'm not clear and my colleagues are not clear either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, never mind. There will be other opportunities, Your Honour. We can use the small map, but it is in a very small format and it's very difficult to things on it. Those are aerial photographs. If this were an A3 format, it would be much easier to examine the witness on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have the small map in a larger format, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, actually, what counsel is holding up is, in fact, the complete map of Sarajevo, from which this inset has been taken. And counsel asked for that and I provided it to him. So I didn't use it in my examination-in-chief. If counsel wants to use it in cross-examination, then maybe counsel should have made copies for that; but If not, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on, please. He has given you his all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to clarify this with the Trial Chamber in writing in order not to take up much more time on this problem, but I will have to explain this in writing, once we have finished hearing this witness, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, you had this training in Zagreb that you referred to, and, anyway, it's your profession. Can you tell us about the shell of 120-millimetres? What does it weigh? I asked many experts, mainly generals, and my information is it weighs two and a half kilos. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct at all. It's far more than two and a half kilos. You would have to specify whether you referring to a 120-millimetre mortar shell or a 120 millimetre artillery shell, but it's the far more than two and a half kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard in my headphones "kilometres. "

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant kilos for kilograms?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So a mortar shell of 120-millimetres weighs how much.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would only be able to give an estimate, but a mortar shell of 120-millimetre would be somewhere between 20 or 30 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did I hear you correctly, 20, 30 kilos? That's the interpretation I got.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that such shells, if they weigh as much as you say they weigh, must be picked up by radars, at least high-quality radars? State of the art radars pick them up after they take off. Already ten metres above the ground, radars pick up everything in the area. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, as an officer, I know that there are equipment that are able to -- to track artillery grenades during the flight, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Anything that is ten metres and over above the ground, above surface?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the specifics of those radars because that is not within the -- my area of competence, and we were certainly not dealing in that during my service in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that British units as well as Dutch units and some other country's units had very high quality radars at the time of the tragic event at Markale on the 28th of August. Are you aware of that as a member of the team which investigated this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that British forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a small point for clarification. The witness has not said that he was a member of the team that investigated this, in other words, the 28th of August incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he did say that. I'm not going to pinpoint him on any of his words, but I think he said he was a member of that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I was a member of the military observer team that conducted the investigation on the 28th of August on the market-place. My position was on the OP1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it the case that it's almost impossible, in view of the equipment positioned in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo, that the sound of any projectile not be picked up? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have heard so many mortar and artillery rounds firing during my career, so I would have heard if there was any outgoing round from the area within my observation post, referring to the incident on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you something else. There were devices to monitor the sounds of incoming and outcoming projectiles. Not a single sound monitoring instrument registered that projectile, that shell as it was coming in. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a military observer. I didn't have access to any other devices other than my eye, my ears, and my binoculars, so I can't comment on any other kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But if you participated in this work by observing everything that happened on that tragic day, did you come across this piece of information; namely, that not a single instrument picked up the sound of that shell as it was coming in?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask the Registrar to show DD0-05-10 [as interpreted]; namely, the statement of Mr. Knustad dated 21st of May, 1996 [as interpreted], to show it on the screens. I want to confront the witness with some of the passages from his statement of the 21st of May, 1999 [as interpreted]. DD00-0510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask the witness to focus on the fourth paragraph on page 3 in English. It begins with the words: "On the morning of 28th August."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to read it all. But just one sentence in the middle of that paragraph: "Then I heard the sound of an impact explosion somewhere in the city; and from my experience, my first thoughts were that it sounded like a mortar impact." Is that correct? Is that correctly reflected?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, you say: "I heard only one impact, and I know that the mortar had not passed close to our position because I would have heard it. I can also say that if the mortar had been fired from within the confrontation line, I would have heard that, too. All the area surrounding the confrontation line was controlled by Serbs." Does that correctly reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does and that reflects what is I said, that I didn't hear any outgoing mortar rounds from within the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, the reason I'm asking all this is the last paragraph: "Paul and I filled out the UNMO incident which explained fully what we had observed. We then reported the same incident by radio to the duty officer at the military observers headquarters for Sector Sarajevo. That was the end of my involvement with that particular incident, as I was not called upon to investigate the site of the impact." Is that correct, that you had no longer any involvement in that investigation, as I understand from this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this refers to the actual incident that occurred on that day. And the whole meaning about the last sentence is that I was not called to go down from the OP1 to the impact site and contribute in the -- in the investigation on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, we can, therefore, conclude that you saw the shell impact and that you didn't know anything else and you reported to the headquarters accordingly. You only saw the smoke and the shell impact; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and that's what I have stated earlier. I saw the smokestack, I heard the sound of the impact, and I was able to confirm which area that impact was. And we reported that according to the procedures to our UNMO headquarters and as well logged it as -- as I stated in -- in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order for us not to go back to the statement again, I would like to call up page 2 of your statement to our screens; namely, of your statement. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There you speak of Sedrenik, and you say exactly what you told us today. You said that one can see the entire town clearly from Sedrenik; the centre of town and everything there, because the vantage point is on the hill.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I said that referring to the OP1 and not about the team base we had in Sedrenik, and Sedrenik is on the total opposite side, to the northern side of the old part of the city. The OP1, that I was referring to regarding the good visibility, is on the southern part of the old part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my mistake. But from that vantage point, one can clearly see downtown Sarajevo and all the different points can easily be controlled this way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the team base in Sedrenik or the OP in Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about Colina Kapa, not the place that you were at that you drew on the map a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I drew on the map was Colina Kapa and the observation point. I think that's quite clear on the -- the map. It shows Colina Kapa, and there is nothing mentioned there about Sedrenik. I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that I was mistaken myself, but let's talk about Colina Kapa. It's some 940 metres high; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the city of Sarajevo is approximately only 600 metres above sea level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And Colina Kapa lies at 940 metres above sea level.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's on the top of Colina Kapa; but as I have stated, the OP itself was a bit further north from the top of Colina Kapa, down on the -- on the slope towards the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that Colina Kapa, which is part of Trebevic and is 940 metres high, was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was under control of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, as I stated, and we had the front line of the Bosnian army approximately 150 to 200 metres south of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from that vantage point, you have Sarajevo as if it were on the palm of your hand, as we say in our language, and many witnesses testified to that effect here.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's a magnificent view especially of the old part of the city from that observation point. And from a military perspective, of course, there was no coincidence that the UN observation point was placed exactly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, it is at a somewhat lower level to that where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had its positions?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to direct you to paragraph 5 now, and that's the reason why I called up this map. You say that Kevin Curtis from ICTY has shown you a map of the Sarajevo area in two parts, and now I'm quoting. "On those maps, I have drawn, to the best my recollection, in green ink, the confrontation line as it was then." Can you tell us which confrontation line did you, indeed, draw as you arrived Sarajevo toward the end of the war? Can you show the line to us on this map here? Which were those lines?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are confrontation line that we had on our maps that we used during our duty as military observers. It showed the middle of the confrontation line between the Bosnian army and the Serb army. As -- as stated, there is a no man's land in between, and we would, for our knowledge, draw the confrontation line as the middle of the no man's land.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us the line on the map here? Just indicate it, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was Colina Kapa? Can you show it to us. It was within the area of responsibility? What does the blue line stand for?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that blue line is the army of ABiH-held territory and -- on the outskirts of that one. So to my understanding, this blue dotted line shows the front line of the army of BiH, and the red dotted line shows the front line of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you, at least, roughly show us the place where you were stationed, Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so I can easily follow, could the camera be focussed on the map while the witness is pointing to it, because it's difficult for me here to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the camera be focussed so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Colina Kapa was within the area of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If indeed it was within the area of control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then it should be behind that blue line there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't validate the correctness of this map, and I don't know when it's dated because the confrontation line, it changed. But I knew understand that the end station of the cable car going up to Colina Kapa was Bosnian Serb-held territory, and that's just to the east of our position on Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, mountains are never small affairs. I asked you about the top of Colina Kapa a moment ago, and you said that the tip of Colina Kapa was indeed within the area controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The knowledge that I had was that the Bosnian government army was at the top of Colina Kapa and that Bosnian Serb army was further south than that. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you arrived in Sarajevo only in the month of June, you perhaps cannot tell you [as interpreted] that, but do you know of any other confrontation lines between the two armies in addition to this one. Could you tell us what these blue and red lines stand for? Did you learn this information during your time there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly know what blue and red lines indicate on this map, and I just explained that in previous answer. On our maps in -- that we used as military observers, we had one line, indicating the middle between the two front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do the blue lines represent the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the red lines those of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, as I see it on this map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you extensively spoke of aerial bombs. There is no need to repeat your words. Firstly, I'm interested in the following: You said that they are quite slow. Would -- were they so slow that the people seeing the bomb arriving would have enough time to take shelter, a minute or two later, before the impact that took place a minute or two later?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
