utterances.text: No. That would hardly be possible. You would be able to see it if you were on a close distance and you saw it fired and then you would see it pass by in front of you on the distance, let's say, up to a few hundred metres, between 4 and 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If a bomb came from the positions of the army of Republika Srpska, which were some two to three kilometres away, then they were quite visible as they were quite noisy and flying quite slow. People would have enough time to take shelter, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they wouldn't. And I have seen myself one of these weapons fired from Sharpstone. I saw it being prepared. My position was at the team based in Sedrenik. I saw it being prepared on Sharpstone and fired towards the centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you do not allow for the possibility that the bomb could have been fired by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in view of the confrontation lines as you drew them. You do not allow for this possibility?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we now talking about the aerial bombs from Sharpstone, or are we talking about anything fired from within the vicinity of OP1?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: As you are quite familiar with these aerial bombs and you observed them, do you exclude the possibility that this aerial bomb was, in fact, launched from the Sharpstone where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was stationed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I conclude that completely since I witnessed this with my own eyes, and it was very easy to know actually where the confrontation lines were in the Sharpstone area. And we had very good control of the Bosnian Serb sniper position on the Sharpstone, and we knew it was Bosnian Serb territory since they always made sure that the Bosnian Serb flag was on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the following: This is a document that I will be showing to someone else, but it is authored by UNPROFOR, wherein, UNPROFOR had insisted on the setting up of an observation post on Sharpstone and that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina continuously refused to allow that. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are categorical in claiming that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina never, ever fired one such bomb during your time there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not categorical. I'm just referring to what I observed and what we reported, and I have stated that I did not see any mortars or any other weapons fired from the Bosnian government forces within the confrontation line. Besides that, we were very well aware of the fact that government army did not have very much heavy weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you state that categorically?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask that DD00-0510 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D57, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the UNPROFOR document that I referred to but did not quote from, I will need to show the entire document to Mr. Knustad. That is DD00-0463, which is listed as, or rather, as admitted as D31. This is a report by the UNMO headquarters for Sector Sarajevo concerning the events taking place on the 28th of June, 1995, and the TV building related events in Sarajevo. This is just one document in addition to two others that I will be using. Can I ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document I have listed as DD00-0463 is -- is not listed as D31. What I have list as D31 is a different document. Can counsel clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to call DD00-0463 then, because it is in e-court. I think it's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the document? I would like to show it to you in its entirety. It was sent by UNMO headquarters, Sector Sarajevo. You see the date there 1995, prepared by Captain T. Hansen, operations officer, and release by Lieutenant-Colonel Alan, a deputy officer. Is that right? Deputy commander; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. Deputy commander of the military observers. That is something else other than UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I have never been a soldier, myself. I was even relieved from duty. To inform UNPROFOR in Zagreb. Subject, special report on impact in TV building in June 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please give me yes or no answers, so we go through this quickly. It goes on to say, "In June, an UNMO coming into the PTT buildings parking his car on the lower parking place observed the following." Is this correctly reflected? Am I saying what is written here?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. I haven't seen this report before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please answer with a yes or no. There is no need for to you give any explanations. Heard and saw an outgoing projectile across the parking place and road, from grid such-and-such a number. The place is on the BiH territory, approximately 1800 metres from the nearest confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what the report says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' correction: Not confrontation line but cease-fire line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The dust was seen and a low flying projectile heading towards the TV building. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The projectile was following a low trajectory, travelling directly from firing point to target, and hit the TV building on the northern side facing the British Cymbelline building; that is to say, equipment for monitoring mortar fire. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The projectile was a short one. The width was quite big, 20 centimetre or more. The length was approximately 60 centimetres or more. Is that right? Is that the text you see there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no smoke observed whilst the low trajectory object was in flight. The velocity speed was quite sluggish.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That is what the report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The explosion was a few seconds after the impact. It looked quite heavy. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, this is a report prepared by somebody else. He is merely confirming what is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will finish quite soon, and I wish to tender this into evidence. One other military observer saw some other matters that completed the picture, but never mind. This was described in the indictment, and we've had people testifying here that this was this Krmaca bomb that hit the TV building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Having seen this, does the witness deny the fact that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had these launchers that could have been used to fire such a projectile such as an aerial bomb, or does he stand by his categorical assertion even after seeing this report. This is my question for him.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm and state what I have seen and heard, and my statement was that I never saw any rounds being fired with heavy weapons from within the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the one that arrived from Sharpstone for which you categorically claimed that it was fired from the positions of the army of Republika Srpska, whereas, both sides had their positions there? Do you now still exclude the possibility that the projectile may have been fired by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I exclude that because we were well aware of where the confrontation lines were in the vicinity of Sharpstone. And, as I stated, I saw it with my own eyes, and the Bosnian Serb army had the territory on the top of the Sharpstone. The government army had the area below, towards Grdonja, the hill just south-west of Sharpstone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see on the screen another two documents, and I will be through with this. DD00-0506. That's a report on a telephone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, just so I understand things better, this report that you just read and that had been drafted by other witness. According to you, this report means that an air bomb had been launched by the ABiH army from that building. Is that how you understand this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You recall quite correctly that I have shown this report to a protected witness, and on that occasion I presented an assertion that this Trial Chamber will judge on, in due course. It was indeed fired from a distance of several hundred metres from the TV building, according to that document, but I'm not going to go into the details now. As for what happened at the TV building, I can even go as far as to say that an explosive device had been set in that building that created all the havoc we've seen. If that is what you are asking, I can even say that the explosion that created so much damage without wounding anyone, apart from the corpse of the man who died, God knows where. I do assert that it was fired from several hundred metres of the target. It ricocheted three times without exploding, so not that the explosive device was set up within the building. It flew in and it was seen by none other than a high ranking officer of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you would like the witness to confirm what you have understood? It seems that that is the problem, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, Your Honour. I'm just saying that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina used those large bombs that we call "sows" in our language, that they were in possession of the same kind of bombs and represented their own act as a misdeed of the army of Republika Srpska. This witness is saying that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina never fired a bomb of this kind. So I'm asking you if he continues to believe that, after having seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this. Is it your evidence that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina never fired an air bomb called a "sow," or is it your evidence that you never witnessed such a firing by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My statement is that I never witnessed it. I wouldn't be able to -- to confirm whether it was used, and I did not witness it. So I am not categorically that it was never fired, but I never witnessed it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever hear any reports of such a firing by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not hear of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my final question regarding this. Maybe he did not hear about it before, but he is hearing about it now. Does he allow the possibility that this sow bomb from Sharpstone was fired by somebody other than the army of Republika Srpska. The Court will, of course, deliberate on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you, Witness, absolutely exclude the possibility that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina used projectiles of this kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has already answered this question, in as much as it relates to the general proposition that ABiH fire these projectiles. I don't know whether the question relates specifically to the incident at Sharpstone, which the witness has been given about. Perhaps that could be clarified. But if it is the former, then I submit that the witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will allow the question. What is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have stated, we were very well aware of where the confrontation lines were in the Sharpstone area. We knew that the Sharpstone, the top of the hill was Bosnian Serb-head army territory, and I have stated that I saw modified air bomb being fired from that position. I only state what I observed and what I heard. I also stated that I observed a Bosnian Serb flag on the top of the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it is necessary to carry on with this issue. The witness has said what he said, and it is ultimately up to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Tell me, Mr. Sachdeva, the report which was just shown to the witness and which is marked for identification, you know it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D31. Is it the intention of the Prosecution to call the person who prepared that report, the army officer who prepared that report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the person who prepared the report is not currently on the Prosecution witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I would imagine, then, that the Defence will want to call that person. If neither side is calling the person who wrote that report -- let me finish. If neither side is going to call that person who wrote that report, then I will call that person as a witness of the Court because we must hear from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I just add that he was on the Prosecution witness list. However, upon our review of the military records in Banja Luka, wherein, we -- we identified the document that was tendered through witness 138 a couple of weeks ago, a document of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and of, allegedly, the accused stating that his troops had hit the TV building, it was decided that we would move with that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Have you completed your cross-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did abbreviate a lot, but I have a couple of matters outstanding, a couple of more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly, this document is D31, isn't it? I mean marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what document you are referring to, but D31 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's correct. I have indictment DD00-0463, marked for identification, is D31 on the 1st of February. However, just a point of clarification. That is marked for identification and not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never received from the Prosecution the information report regarding Mr. Knustad dated 2nd October, 2003. It was marked DD00-0506. But since it is already on the screen, I would like to examine the witness on the paragraph titled, "impact."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Knustad was in the post with an Irish army officer," who is named. "They compared their observations and came to the conclusion that the mortar round had impacted the area of Markale and that neither had detected the sound of the round being fired within the area that they could see and here." Thus, neither Mr. Conway, the Irish officer, nor you heard the sound; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that neither of you heard the sound of another four or five shells and that neither of you noticed them or could see their impact and their effect?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had heard or seen, observed, another impacts, we would have reported it. In this case, we observed and heard one impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have document DD00-0506 also exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D58, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to clarify, counsel appeared to suggest that this information report had not been disclosed, when in fact the English was disclosed on the 25th of May, 2006 and the B/C/S was disclosed on the 6th of February, 2007, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that I made that mistake, but that's the document. Actually, I don't understand what this is about. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness another exhibit that was admitted a long time ago, one of the most important for Markale. DD00-0010. It's a report from the 28th of August addressed by General Janvier to the competent representatives of the command of the UN Peace Corps and to Secretary-General Annan himself. Can we see the English page number 3? UNPROFOR, Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please read this passage, so that my following questions will not confuse him. Until the end of that first paragraph. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the report from the 28th, day one, and it says, "Concerning mortar shells. Definition of firing positions for mortar rounds is very difficult because it is impossible to determine the level charge used to fire the projectiles." Can you confirm that this indeed very difficult?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is and that is as well in line with the -- my statement. We can only indicate from which direction we evaluated that it was fired, and it is difficult to say at what distance. But in this case, we -- I have already stated that nothing was fired as we observed from within the confrontation line and that sector that I drew on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You neither heard it nor saw it? I mean, you didn't hear or see anything but what you described.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have stated what I have saw and what I heard already, one impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was waiting for the opportunity to ask you this. Below it says: "For the most part, in Ilidza, Butmir, Dobrinja, the maximum concentration of impacts was reported in the area of Debelo Brdo and Grbavica. An exchange of shelling took place downtown in the afternoon of 28th August. Most of it from the BSA side and this shelling ended with another five rockets towards downtown in the evening. One incident involving the security of UN personnel was reported." Now my question is: How come there is an exchange of mortar fire? You are following the incoming and outcoming rounds and you follow all that, but you did not register at all what happened that same morning?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I did not talk about anything what was registered that morning, I don't understand. I already stated that fact, and I can only state what I what I observed and what I heard. I -- I'm sorry. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How is it possible that all these shells are suddenly both heard and seen and they produce very bad effects on both sides, whereas, everything that transpired the same morning was neither seen nor heard. My question is: Is it possible that explosions were set up in those five locations and that you could only hear the sound of explosions, nothing else? That's what I'm putting to you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a speculation from my side, so I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the ranking officers of NATO, and I have to put it to you, said that they have also wondered about the possibility of the BH army abusing their own troops. I'm not talking conspiracy now, but that possibility was also taken into account by one of the NATO ranking officers. What could you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with all respect to General Janvier, I can neither confirm or not confirm that statement, because I keep very strictly to what I recall that I have observed and what I have reported, and I want to stick to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand why you are mentioning General Janvier. Maybe he referred to that possibility, too. But what I was referring to was a witness we heard sometime ago here, Nicolai, who speculated that this could have been done also by the BH army, to the detriment of their own people?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about that idea, that possibility in the thinking of your personnel.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question, but I can repeat it, repeat it, if that's wanted, to be aware of the fact that there were speculations about rounds being fired from the Bosnian government army within the confrontation line. We were briefed about that, and we were also on our meetings with the Bosnian government army confronted with that fact. But I -- during my service in Sarajevo, I was never able to determine or confirm that anything was fired within the confrontation line by the Bosnian government army that impacted within the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not even the snipers who fired on their own people? You didn't hear about that either?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard speculations about that as well, so that's one more fact that we were very aware of. And this goes again to the impartiality. We had to report what we observed, but I never confirmed that there was any fire from a sniper towards a target inside the confrontation line, and fired by a Bosnian government soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you never heard of official UNPROFOR reports on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did have more questions, but I will end here. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks, Witness. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just about this -- the question of Mr. Tapuskovic concerning the line. I would like to call upon your military experience. You said that you drew on this map which I'm looking, and for the moment I'm keeping it with me. Unfortunately, it can't be put on the -- on the ELMO. You drew the impact of the mortar round on the market of Markale, and the direction whence it came from. And you also showed where OP1 was, your post, OP1. I'm asking you, indeed, because Mr. Tapuskovic tells you that on the same day you heard a lot of other detonations and explosion, if I understood correctly, that shell which arrived on the market you did not hear it nor see it. Therefore, owing to the place where you were and according to your experience, is it possible that this shell might have gone through without being either seen or heard? Taking into account its direction and the impact point, from a strictly military point of view, is it possible, can it be envisaged or not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand the question, if it was possible to see it during the flight. But I can only refer to the fact that I observed something that I identified as an explosion, a detonation from an incoming round in the area of Markale. I saw it, and I heard the sound from the impact. And besides that, of course, there was a lot of other rounds coming in and impacting in the city during that day and other days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any questions. I just want to state the following: I myself did not make any claims. I only referred to what was stated in the report addressed to Kofi Annan that the shells detonated throughout the afternoon and that there was an exchange of shells from both sides, and this is the document that I wanted to use before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think there is no problem. All I wanted was to have some clarifications about the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have two question for you; one relates to your investigation of the Markale incident, and another question which relates in more general terms to the confrontation line. My first question is this: Did you apply your skills in crater analysis to determine that the shell that hit the Markale market that day, that noon on the 28th of August came from that direction 170 degrees, plus/minus 5 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on the impact site that day. Our team leader was the one who actually did the crater analysis and it's investigation at the point of impact, so my contribution to this what I observed from my position in OP1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you did not yourself analyse the craters that landed in the area of Markale that day.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That exhausted my first question. My second question is then regarding the confrontation lines, because we have heard during this trial so far a number of witnesses who have testified about how the confrontation lines were visible. And my question to you is exactly this: If you came to a confrontation line, would you then be able to see it? Were there trenches dug or were there soldiers or combatants posted all along the confrontation line, or how -- how was it possible to demarcate the confrontation lines with such a degree of precision, as we see on this map and as we have seen on others?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it varied actually on the different parts of the city. On some areas, you could actually see what was the forward positions on the both sides, while in other areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. How could you see that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, we could see, from OP1, Serb artillery positions on the hill on the eastern-most part of the city. We observed them every day with the binoculars from our observation post. I can't now remember the name of that hill, but it's the eastern-most hill above the valley of Vasin Han that is in eastern part of Sarajevo. So that was one example. In other parts, it was more unclear and the confrontation line was closer between the -- the forces especially in the urban areas, like Grbavica, for example. So it's very difficult to give a precise answer on that. The only thing I can say is that it was different in different parts of -- of the surrounded city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How close would the front lines be to each other. That would depend on the map. It's still unclear to me how one would be able to determine where exactly the front line was and the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can use Sharpstone as an example, since I know that area very well and that was close to our team base. And in that area, it was less than, well, say, 200 metres from the forward Bosnian government soldier to the forward Serbian army soldier. And it was very clear. While in other areas, they -- they were farther apart from each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, the map that we are looking at, which is behind you and which I presume it will be tendered into evidence, does it accurately reflect the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't state the accuracy of it, because on a lot of those areas I haven't physically been myself when the confrontation line was like to this. But to my best recall, it fits very well with the image that I had of the confrontation line, especially surrounding Sarajevo at the time that I was in the sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the most part, I observe that the line is continuous and unbroken. Does that mean that there were troops throughout the entirety of what is represented by those lines? Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But I wouldn't be able to give an answer on that, since I didn't go personally myself through all the trenches on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I imagine we might hear more about that from other witnesses. Mr. Tapuskovic, without giving any evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I forgot to tender this into evidence. Let me tell you this: When it comes to victim witnesses, they will be the only ones with whom I will not be going through the map. Mr. Knustad, of course, himself cannot speak to that effect, because he only arrived Sarajevo in the month of June of 1995. However, those who were on the front lines and also around Sarajevo will -- and in Sarajevo will be able to talk to this map. I will be presenting the map to every non-victim witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit the map into evidence. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As we do this, can I ask Counsel Tapuskovic, does the map have a date? When was this map or -- drawn, or rather, the lines that are shown on the map, when were they drawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have another map, a similar one, that I will be tendering quite soon dated the 7th of July during the time of Galic. This map here is the map that dates from the time when General Dragomir Milosevic took up his position, from the 10th of August up until the end of the indictment period. And as you can see here, it bears also it's approval of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's large format colour military map will be admitted as Exhibit D59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But I was wondering if we could take the break at this moment, since it is time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Knustad, I just wanted to ask you one question in clarification to His Honour Judge Mindua's question to you a moment ago. If a round had been fired from within the confrontation lines along the flight path of the direction of fire that you indicated on the map, would you have heard that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: At that time on that date, did you hear a round being fired from within the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KNUSTAD [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not hear a round being fired from within the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's the re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Knustad. That concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is going to be taken by Ms. Edgerton. May I please be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I thought my colleague had gone to get the witness. That would be Mr. Agovic, Your Honours. And Mr. Agovic is going to testify about a sniping incident dated 3rd of March, 1995; sniping incident 14, SN 14. And he's a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And would it save any time, Mr. Registrar, if I gave you the first ter number to deal with? That would be 2894.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. And you may begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Azem Agovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What is your present occupation, Mr. Agovic?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Architect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could, I'd like to have PT 2894 on the screen for Mr. Agovic, a statement dated 21 November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Agovic, could you have a look at the documents on the screen in front of you and tell us whether you had an opportunity to review these prior to your testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the English document on the left-hand side of the screen, do you recognise your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recall whether the document was read back to you in your own language before signing it?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then move to the next document, PT 2895. That would be a statement dated 21 April 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Agovic, do you have an opportunity to review both of these documents prior to testifying today?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect to the English one on the left-hand side of the screen, do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this document was read back to you in your own language before signing?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move to one further and final PT number. That would be 00739 at page 10 of that document. Yes, if we could move to page 10, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The page that is on the screen is our e-court page 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could scroll further and identify the page number. Could you go to the preceding page, please. I think in the interests of time, Your Honours, we're able to do without this document, in fact, and we'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Agovic, omitting the document that is on the screen in front of you and referring to your statements to representatives of the OTP in 1995 and 2006, do those two documents constitute an accurate record of what happened to you on March 3rd, 1995?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any additions, deletions, or alterations to make to the information contained in those documents?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then have 2894 and 2895 marked as exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 02894 will become Exhibit P 210. 65 ter number 02895 will become Exhibit P 211.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I have only very few additional questions for you, Mr. Agovic with respect to the information contained in those statements. Do you recall what the weather was like on the day that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: It was a sunny and clear day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As you rode on the tram, were you able to see or did you any military activity at all in the area in which you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, just as one month before, there were no activities. It was a peaceful day. You could hear the birds chirping.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, in particular your 1995 statement, you indicated that the tram you were riding on was headed towards Bascarsija and you were sitting facing the rear of the tram. Now, perhaps you could tell us, as you were sitting, which area of Sarajevo lay to your left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: To my left, there was the Grbavica neighbourhood. I was facing Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what colour of clothes were you wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: I was wearing this very jacket I'm wearing today, 12 years on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Your Honours. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the Defence counsel for Dragomir Milosevic. I will try to clarify some matters with you with reference to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, indeed, I'm ready to cross-examine. However, I heard something that is quite new to me; namely, that Mr. Agovic was wearing this very jacket on the day he was hit. There is something I didn't know. Can he show us where the bullet that wounded him entered his body and where it exited his body? Can he with see that on his jacket? I'm sorry to have to ask this, but having heard this just now I feel duty-bound do ask him that. I'm sure the jacket must show traces of the bullet entering and exiting his body in the hip area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please show this for us?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: Here you can see -- may I stand up? You can see where the bullet entered and it exited here. Here you can see where the bullet entered and passed through here and came out through here. If need be, I can also show it on my person, where the bullet entered and where it exited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't consider that to be necessary. We have -- the witness has indicated where the bullet entered through his jacket and his person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did not the police who were involved in the investigation take the jacket as corpus delecti in order to present it before the courts seized of the matter in Bosnia-Herzegovina or elsewhere. How do you explain the fact that the police did not take the jacket? Did they take any photographs at the time they were taking your statement? Did the police any shots of your jacket at the time, and are there any photographs, contemporaneous photographs indicating that you were hit?

utterances.speaker: AZEM AGOVIC
utterances.text: The police did not take any photographs of either my jacket or me. I was wounded and I was in intensive care. There was no opportunity for them to carry out that on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've -- I almost feel like not asking anything any further. In fact, I will not put a single question to this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter for you decide. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, the problem for us Judges here is to establish the reality of the wound and the shot, as well as the origin and therefore the perpetrator. So I admire how concise you have been in putting all of this to us, but unfortunately, I don't have if my colleagues have a medical report at hand regarding the wound inflicted to this witness. But for the moment, we have no elements to establish the wound and the origin of the shot, the shot that happened while the witness was sitting in the tram. I'm sure you wanted to save time and maybe that is why the counsel for Defence has such a hard time with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please allow Ms. Edgerton to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If it would assist Your Honours in clarification of the extent of the injuries that this witness suffered, we certainly do have medical reports available. However, the witness made it clear in both of his statements that the shot entered the left side of his hip and passed through his body, as he was sitting with his left side facing Grbavica. However, again, as -- if it clarifies the matter for Your Honours, we're happy to provide the parties with the medical documentation for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have the medical reports here, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would be able to make them available first thing tomorrow morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe to help, we already had two witnesses regarding this incident, so we have already tendered this evidence, this report. The police report has already been tendered, and the medical report is included in all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I thank my colleague, Ms. Isailovic. That is absolutely correct Your Honours. If it would assist Your Honours to clarify matters, we could deal with this matter perhaps quite briefly tomorrow and indicate the relevant documentation that has been introduced to date. And at the same time, Your Honour, of course, I would refer to the witness' statements which have now been tendered as exhibits and admitted, in particular paragraphs which deal specifically with the points of origin the fire, the points, landmarks he was passing in Sarajevo at the time he was injured. But I think if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, then, that the witness be brought back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, he would be here in any case because he would not able to travel until tomorrow afternoon. We're in afternoon Court tomorrow, and I was thinking that he would be able to make the afternoon flight tomorrow. I was thinking we were in morning court. I would suggest, Your Honours, you could leave it with us, and I'll make the documentation available to the party, my colleague, tomorrow morning. And we may be able to deal with it quite expeditiously, and we will be able to determine then whether the witness should be brought back. Your Honours, I certainly have no further questions of this witness, keeping in mind what has been put before this Chamber to date about this incident and the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the evidence that you would present?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Together with the medical records which may assist His Honour Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no intention whatsoever to be calculating matters in any way. It was my learned friend's right to ask of him only a couple of questions. I could have been examining him for an hour. I have completed my cross-examination and I will not have any further questions of this witness. If the Trial Chamber will proceed pursuant to the rules of Procedure and Evidence as you have been so far, I don't think there will be any reason for to us be belabour the point. I had not be belabouring it myself as I do not see any reason for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to dismiss the witness. Mr. Agovic, your evidence is concluded. We thank you for giving it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Next witness, Your Honours, is Mr. Bodgan Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this examination-in-chief also takes three minutes, I will have to go home and bring the file because I did not reckon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a procedure here 92 bis and 92 ter, and its purpose is expeditiousness. In no case should a 92 bis or the 92 ter witness take more than 20 minutes, 25 minutes, or half an hour at the most in examination-in-chief. Are you not familiar with the practices here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may our case manager leave the courtroom for a moment to go to the Defence room and bring something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If it is of assistance, my examination -- Is this is not a 92 ter witness. My examination will take -- my guess it will take us close if not beyond the end of day. I don't expect Mr. Tapuskovic to have to start his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to be overly long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I am going to be as concise as I can, Your Honour. I just need immediate a moment to log-in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening. My name is Bodgan Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could ask the assistance of the court officer. If the ELMO could be lowered, it is blocking my view of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I work in the MUP of the Sarajevo Canton, the Department of Crime Scene Officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you join the police?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you joined on that date, did it have the same name, or did you join a different force with a different name?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was called the Security Services Centre. Again, it was the Criminal Forensics Department of the KDZ, that was the full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you joined, what position did you have?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a scene of crime officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber very briefly what your training was.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had a six-month training that included basic training in fingerprinting, criminal investigation of crime scenes, forensic photography, sketching, lectures and courses in biology, chemistry ballistics, and all of the other forensic skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After that six-month training, did you receive any on-the-job training while you were working?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we started actual downsite investigations, at first we were accompanied by senior colleagues who shared their knowledge about the skill of finding clues, traces, and anything that might be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you started working, which would have been after the training, and so I take it would have been in 1993; is that correct? When you actually started working on the job?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the end August 1993 when I first started working as an as a scene of crime officer when I already had my diploma.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to investigate sniping and shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, when I just started working during the war in Bosnia, I attended scenes of shelling and sniping incidents that were common at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you continue to live and work in Sarajevo from -- during the entire period from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the entire duration of the war, I was in Sarajevo working on the same job, which I continued after the war, to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you went to a scene where a sniping or a shelling had occurred, could you describe for the Trial Chamber briefly what were your specific duties?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my duties in a on-site investigation were to find traces; if any; photographs; collecting clues and traces; bagging them; and taking them for further forensic examination, if that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you right reports about your on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After each on-site investigation was performed, a report would be written and a photographic file would be prepared, including a sketch of the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In terms of sniping -- the degree or volume of sniping and shelling, could you compare for us the period of 1992 until August of 1994, compare that period to the period August 1994 to November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was no great difference in the degree of shelling, although perhaps the worst shelling was during 1995, especially the summer of that year. It's hard to say, really. It was bad throughout. But I believe 1995, the spring and summer of that year were the worst in terms of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about sniping? Was sniping the same throughout or were there periods - let me finish the question - or were their periods that were worse than other periods?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, there was sniping incidents, but, again, the end of spring and the summer of 1995 were the hardest for Sarajevo, in terms of shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I lived and I still live in an apartment in the centre of Sarajevo, Radiceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In October of 1992, did you live with your father there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did something happen to him in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed on the 6th of October, 1992 as a result of shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was he when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some 25 to 50 metres away from our flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was he doing at the time he was killed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was coming back from getting water from a water-tank parked close to our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How old was he when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fifty-six.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us approximately how many shells fell on your street during the war?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we take only the area around my apartment building, around 50 shells fell in the vicinity of that single location, maybe more. That's as far as I was able to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say during -- when you described those 50 shells, is that during the entire period of the war from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there any military facility or installation on your street or near your street?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from my workplace, the Security Services Centre was close to my building, currently the MUP of the Sarajevo Canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were this period of times when there were members of the police that were engaged in fighting, in military activity?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was happening at the beginning of the war in 1992 until I can't say exactly when it stopped, but I believe it was sometime in 1993, in fact, until the establish am of the BH army as it existed later on in the war. After that, they were withdrawn to their regular duties they continued to perform until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And after that occurred, that you say occurred in 1993, did shells continue to fall on your street?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was there any neighbourhood in Sarajevo where sniping was more of a problem than other neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to single out a single neighbourhood, expect maybe for the line from Marindvor, which was constantly under fire, and there is a crossroads, an intersection about 100 or 150 metres from Marindvor which was known in Sarajevo was the Hygienic Institute intersection, and that whole line from Marindvor to that was under constant sniping fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know where this constant sniping fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It came from positions that, as I heard from others, were held by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know where those were located?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, speaking of Marindvor, they were in a part of town called Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn specifically any -- of any locations where snipers were known to have be firing from, from Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a building known as Metalka, and there were also sky-scrapers from the top of which sniper fire came.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber how did you learn this information? How did this information come to you about where the sniper fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mainly from eye-witnesses who were shot at from those buildings and from my personal experience also, because one had to be very careful passing through those areas. You could always hear shooting from that direction, from the direction of those two -- of those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This information, are you able to tell us if this is information that was known only to the police, like yourselves, or was this information that was commonly known?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was commonly known. I don't think there's a single resident of Sarajevo who would not be aware of those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there any measures that were taken to protect against snipers?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Large metal containers were propped up at those intersections that would allow people to have some cover when passing through, because there was no other way to go from one part of the town to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These containers, did they face the Serb positions or the Bosnian army positions?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were at intersections providing cover to civilians passing through and their other side faced Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they effective?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they were; sometimes not. Sometimes a bullet would go right through the container and hit somebody. Sometimes they also shot over them and pedestrians were protected only to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your investigations of sniper cases. Are you able to tell us, approximately, how many sniping cases you investigating during the war? Is that something you're able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, quite a few, but I couldn't give you an exact number now; approximately, 20 cases which I worked on myself and maybe more, because some of my colleagues did the same kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how many of those cases occurred after August of 1994, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After August 1994, well, I really don't know the exact number. I believe I did five on-site investigations, or maybe between five and ten, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the period August 1994 to November of 1995, did you have occasion to investigate shootings on trams, sniping shootings on trams?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did such investigations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On those occasions, were you able to determine the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the tram was on its rails when it was hit, then it was possible to determine the direction of fire. If the tram was abandoned, then based on eye-witness reports and the direction in which the tram had been moving, we would try to establish the direction of fire. It turned out to be mostly from the cemetery above Grbavica and from Grbavica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the -- did you ever have occasion to investigate a sniping incident where you determined that the direction of fire was from Bosnian army forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion -- I'll put the same question about shelling, even though I'm going to ask you some questions about shelling. Did you ever have occasion where you investigating a shelling incident where you determined that the direction of fire was from Bosnian army forces?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's move to -- let's move to shelling incidents. Are you able to estimate after -- from -- in the period of August 1994 to November of 1995 how many shelling incidents you investigated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A lot. I could not even approximate the number. In one day -- there were days when we did six or seven on-site investigations of shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there a month, any particular month that had more shelling investigations than any other that you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I think the summer of 1995 was the period of the greatest number of shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is that when you would sometimes have days with six or seven on-site investigations? Was that also in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's approximately in that period, although such things could have happened even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you're talking about the summer of 1995, are you able to tell us more specifically what months you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: July and August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, regarding the shelling and the sniping incidents, can you tell us -- and, again, stay focussed on this period of August of 1994 until November of 1995, can you tell us approximately what percentage of them this casualties?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I could not really state a percentage, but there were many such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether it was most of the cases or some of the cases, give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't -- let's say it was half, half.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. To the best of your recollection, was there ever an occasion when a casualty of a sniping incident or of a shelling incident that you investigated was that of a uniformed soldier? Do you ever remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe there were some casualties who were in uniform, but whether they were civilians at that particular moment or soldiers, it's hard to say. In most cases, though, the casualties were civilians, or maybe the person just happened to wearing a uniform at the time when they were in the street. At the time, there was a deficit of everything and people were running short of clothing, and they put on anything that could -- they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that "in most cases, though, the casualties were civilians," does that -- are those most cases where -- in those most cases, were the civilians wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever investigate a shelling of a military location?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did your team, your investigation team, ever come under fire while you were conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It happened several times, although for the most part there was shooting, from everywhere, everywhere, all the time, and it was never certain whether we would be able to conduct the investigation or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific occasions when you came under fire during an investigation?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When a shell hit the Holiday Inn hotel and we went out onto the roof of the so-called National Restaurant, that was part of the hotel, to collect the evidence, and then a sniper started shooting at us. Fortunately, no one was hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was, I think, in Autumn of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My final question before we take the break for the evening. Were you able to tell where the sniping was coming from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were fired at from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We'll break until tomorrow afternoon, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of February, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.
